Expert parallelism is commonly used to distribute expert computation across GPUs, while attention-FFN disaggregation (AFD) further improves serving efficiency by separating attention and feed-forward computation into independent worker pools. However, we observe that a naive AFD implementation could make expert load imbalance more harmful: once FFN computation becomes an independent pipeline stage, overloaded experts directly slow the FFN stage and degrade end-to-end serving performance. To solve this problem, we present Afore , a timely expert reconfiguration system for AFD-based MoE serving. Afore exploits two architectural properties of AFD. First, AFD exposes the expert-token distribution of upcoming microbatches before they reach FFN execution, enabling placement decisions based on near-future demand instead of stale historical profiles. Second, AFD creates a pipeline window in which expert migration for a target microbatch can be overlapped with the computation of preceding in-flight microbatches. Based on these insights, Afore formulates expert reconfiguration as a microbatch-aware scheduling problem and uses a migration-aware scheduler to decide when and which experts to migrate. Afore further implements lightweight demand prefetching and NVLink-based GPU-GPU expert migration to reduce reconfiguration overhead. Evaluation on a 110B-parameter MoE model across four dynamic workloads shows that Afore improves output throughput by 10.1–17.6% and reduces P95 inter-token latency by 7.1–9.5% compared with the strongest competing baseline. Compared with static placement, Afore improves throughput by 29.8% on average and reduces P95 inter-token latency by 18.2% on average. Migration profiling further shows that AFD pipeline overlap can fully hide expert-migration latency. 1 Introduction Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are increasingly used by deployed large-scale large language model (LLM) services, including interactive assistants, coding copilots, search, data analysis, enterprise automation, and agentic applications [ 9 , 14 , 8 , 17 , 5 , 29 ] . By activating only a small subset of experts for each token, MoE models increase model capacity while keeping per-token computation manageable [ 15 , 9 ] . However, serving MoE inference at scale remains costly: expert parameters are large, expert activation is input-dependent, and workloads change over time [ 21 , 12 , 10 ] , where the existing solutions are not sufficient. For example, expert parallelism (EP) distributes experts across GPUs to scale expert execution [ 21 ] , and attention-FFN disaggregation (AFD) [ 32 ] further improves resource utilization by separating attention and feed-forward computation into distinct worker pools. Yet in AFD, skewed expert routing directly bottlenecks the independent FFN stage, creates pipeline backpressure, and degrades end-to-end serving performance. In this paper, we explore how to reduce dynamic expert-load imbalance in AFD-based MoE serving without incurring reconfiguration overhead that erodes the resulting performance gains. Addressing this problem is essential because the efficiency of MoE serving increasingly determines the cost and responsiveness of production LLM services [ 12 , 13 , 21 , 11 ] . As modern MoE models grow and workloads become more heterogeneous, small inefficiencies in expert execution can translate into substantial GPU underutilization, reduced output throughput, and higher tail latency [ 14 , 17 , 29 , 13 , 11 , 4 ] . AFD makes this issue especially consequential: once FFN computation is isolated as a separate pipeline stage, imbalance among expert workers can throttle the entire serving pipeline rather than remaining a localized execution inefficiency [ 32 , 2 , 25 , 23 ] . Addressing FFN-side expert imbalance is therefore essential for realizing the scalability benefits of AFD while preserving the latency guarantees required by interactive LLM applications [ 32 , 2 , 25 , 13 , 11 ] . The key system obstacle is that the existing techniques for scaling MoE serving improve capacity and resource utilization but do not remove the dynamic imbalance that arises from input-dependent expert routing . First , EP partitions expert parameters and computation across GPUs, enabling large expert layers to exceed the memory and compute capacity of a single device [ 21 , 12 , 11 , 13 ] ; however, such an approach also makes expert placement and resource allocation central to performance, because GPUs hosting popular experts become stragglers while others remain underutilized. This imbalance is difficult to avoid statically: different requests, layers, and generation phases can activate substantially different experts, producing the skewed expert-load distributions shown in Figure 1 and across-layer imbalance shown in the left panel of Figure 2 . Figure 1 : Left: Expert routing load in a representative AFD window. With top- k = 8 k=8 , a small set of hot experts receives a disproportionate fraction of routed tokens. Right: The resulting load across eight EP workers under static expert placement, where the most loaded worker reaches 2.5 × \times the average load. Figure 2 : Left: EP load imbalance across MoE layers on ShareGPT, with the most imbalanced layer reaching 3.3 × \times imbalance of the average worker load. Right: Normalized throughput under synthetic uniform and skewed routing. Skewed routing reduces throughput by 11.9% under monolithic attention-FFN execution and by 20.1% under AFD. Second , AFD provides a complementary architecture by separating attention and FFN computation into independently provisioned worker pools [ 32 , 23 , 25 , 2 ] , but this separation makes the FFN/expert stage a distinct pipeline bottleneck rather than merely one component of monolithic execution. To examine the performance impact of routing skew, we compare synthetic uniform and skewed routing under monolithic attention-FFN execution and AFD. As shown in the right panel of Figure 2 , skewed routing reduces normalized throughput by 11.9% under monolithic execution and by 20.1% under AFD. Thus, existing scalability mechanisms address model capacity and coarse resource provisioning, but they are insufficient for handling rapidly changing expert-load skew: an overloaded FFN worker in AFD slows the independent FFN stage, creates pipeline bubbles, backpressures the attention stage, and degrades end-to-end serving performance. A natural approach to mitigating expert load imbalance is by reconfiguration, which adjusts expert placement according to runtime load [ 11 , 27 , 22 ] . Reconfiguration can improve expert utilization and reduce stragglers, but existing reconfiguration mechanisms face two fundamental challenges: • C1: Dynamic and unpredictable demand. Expert demand changes over time because token routing depends on the input workload, model layer, sequence position, and request mix [ 4 , 13 ] . Static placement, historical statistics, or coarse-grained profiling can capture only average or past expert popularity; they cannot reliably describe the expert-token distribution of upcoming execution [ 11 , 18 ] . As a result, reconfiguration decisions may react too late or optimize for stale load patterns. • C2: Non-negligible system overhead. Expert reconfiguration introduces runtime overhead from placement scheduling, expert-weight migration, routing-metadata updates, and worker coordination [ 22 , 27 ] . If these operations are exposed on the critical path, the cost of reconfiguration can offset its load-balancing benefit and even degrade overall performance [ 1 , 24 ] . Our key observation is that AFD, while making expert imbalance more harmful, also provides two architectural opportunities for addressing these challenges. In particular, AFD both amplifies expert imbalance and exposes the temporal structure needed to fix it. • O1: Microbatch-level demand is visible. AFD processes requests by a disaggregated microbatch pipeline, where a target microbatch is handled by the attention side before reaching the FFN/expert side [ 32 ] . This pipeline structure exposes the expert-token distribution of the target microbatch before its FFN execution. Therefore, reconfiguration decisions can use near-future demand already available in the pipeline, enabling timely expert placement adaptation under dynamic workloads (addressing C1 ). • O2: reconfiguration overhead can be overlapped. AFD creates a pipeline window between observing the target microbatch’s expert demand and executing that microbatch on the FFN/expert side [ 32 , 23 ] . During this window, preceding in-flight microbatches continue executing on FFN workers. This pipeline structure allows expert migration for the target microbatch to overlap with preceding microbatch computation, reducing the migration overhead exposed on the critical path (addressing C2 ). Based on these insights, we present Afore to accelerate MoE inference serving by a ttention– F FN disaggregation with o verlapped r econfiguration of e xperts. Afore adapts expert placement over time using microbatch-level expert-demand information and overlaps expert migration with the computation of preceding in-flight microbatches. At its core, Afore treats expert reconfiguration as a microbatch-aware scheduling problem: for each target microbatch, the system estimates the FFN-stage imbalance under the current placement, evaluates candidate expert-placement changes, and triggers migration only when the expected reduction in FFN bottlenecks outweighs the migration overhead exposed on the critical path. This design improves FFN-stage balance and end-to-end serving efficiency under dynamic workloads. Our contributions are summarized as follows: Contribution 1: We formulate temporal expert reconfiguration in AFD-based MoE serving as an online expert-placement scheduling problem. The problem jointly determines when to adjust expert placement and which experts to migrate for upcoming microbatches, while accounting for both near-future expert demand and exposed migration overhead. To solve this problem efficiently, we design a migration-aware scheduling algorithm that uses prefetched expert-token distributions to estimate FFN-stage imbalance, evaluates the benefit of candidate placement changes, and performs reconfiguration only when it reduces the critical-path cost of FFN execution. Contribution 2: We design and implement Afore with runtime support for microbatch-level demand prefetching and efficient expert migration. Afore introduces a lightweight prefetching interface that collects the expert-token distribution of target microbatches before they reach FFN execution, enabling placement decisions based on near-future demand. Afore overlaps expert migration with the computation of preceding in-flight microbatches and applies placement updates at microbatch boundaries to avoid disrupting ongoing execution. To reduce migration time, Afore uses NVLink-based GPU-GPU expert transfer for fast expert reconfiguration. Contribution 3: We evaluate Afore on a 110B-parameter MoE model (i.e., GLM-4.5-Air) under four dynamic serving workloads and compare Afore against static placement, statistics-based reconfiguration, reactive load-balancing, and prediction-based reconfiguration baselines. Experimental results show that Afore improves output throughput by 10.1–17.6% and reduces P95 inter-token latency by 7.1–9.5% compared with the strongest competing baseline. Component-wise ablation shows that Afore improves throughput by 29.8% on average and reduces P95 inter-token latency by 18.2% on average over static placement. Migration profiling further shows that AFD pipeline overlap can fully hide expert-migration latency. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. § 2 provides background and related work. § 3 presents the motivation for temporal expert reconfiguration in AFD-based MoE serving. § 4 introduces the overall architecture of Afore . § 5 presents the scheduling framework for expert reconfiguration. § 6 describes the system design and runtime implementation. § 7 presents the system evaluation. § 8 concludes the paper. 2 Background and Related Work Expert parallelism for MoE deployment. MoE models improve the parameter efficiency of LLMs by activating only a small subset of experts for each token [ 15 , 9 , 8 , 14 , 5 , 17 , 29 ] . This sparse activation enables larger parameter space without a proportional increase in per-token computation, which also makes serving more complex because expert parameters and expert computation must be distributed across devices. Recent MoE serving systems commonly rely on expert parallelism to partition experts across GPUs and dispatch tokens to the corresponding expert workers [ 12 , 13 , 21 ] . For instance, FastMoE [ 12 ] and Tutel [ 13 ] optimize distributed expert execution and token dispatch; DeepSpeed-MoE [ 21 ] provides system support for large-scale MoE training and inference; and recent large MoE models further increase the need for efficient expert-parallel serving [ 14 , 17 , 29 ] . These systems establish expert parallelism as a standard mechanism for scaling MoE deployment. However, expert-parallel performance depends heavily on expert placement and resource allocation, since uneven expert activation could lead to serious stragglers. Our work builds on expert-parallel MoE serving and studies how expert placement should be adapted when the FFN/expert stage is deployed under AFD. Attention-FFN disaggregation. A separate thread of effort improves LLM serving by disaggregating computation components with different resource requirements [ 32 , 25 , 2 , 23 ] . In AFD, attention and feed-forward computation are placed on separate worker pools so that each side can be provisioned and optimized independently. This design is motivated by the different bottlenecks of the two stages: attention execution is bounded by KV-cache and other relevant memory access, while FFN execution is dominated by dense or expert MLP computation. Recent AFD systems study how to organize the disaggregated pipeline, transfer intermediate activations, and allocate resources between attention and FFN workers [ 32 , 25 , 2 ] . These works show that AFD is a promising architecture for scalable LLM serving. Our work focuses on maintaining efficient MoE serving under the AFD architecture, where the FFN side may contain expert-parallel computation and its load balance directly affects the service rate of the disaggregated pipeline. MoE workload dynamics and expert-load imbalance. Expert-load imbalance is an essential challenge in MoE serving systems because token routing is input-dependent [ 15 , 9 , 13 , 11 , 4 ] . Different requests, layers, and generation phases can activate different subsets of experts, causing some experts to receive far more tokens than others. Prior work addresses this issue from several angles [ 28 , 26 ] . MoE model designs use auxiliary load-balancing losses or routing constraints to encourage more uniform expert usage [ 15 , 9 ] ; systems such as Tutel optimize token dispatch and communication under skewed activation [ 13 ] ; and expert-placement or prediction methods exploit routing statistics to reduce load skew and communication overhead [ 11 , 4 , 18 ] . These techniques reduce imbalance, but they generally rely on training-time regularization, static placement, or historical runtime feedback. In contrast, Afore targets serving-time expert-load dynamics under AFD by leveraging the disaggregated microbatch pipeline to make expert-placement decisions with timely workload information. MoE expert reconfiguration. Expert reconfiguration dynamically changes expert placement, replication, or resource allocation to adapt to runtime load [ 11 , 27 , 22 , 1 , 24 , 18 ] . For example, placement-oriented systems optimize the mapping between experts and GPUs to reduce load imbalance and communication cost [ 11 ] ; elastic MoE systems adjust expert resources under changing workloads [ 22 , 27 ] ; and online balancing mechanisms migrate or redistribute experts to avoid persistent hot spots [ 24 , 18 ] . These approaches demonstrate the value of adapting expert resources at runtime. However, reconfiguration also introduces overhead that can offset the benefit of load balancing and even degrade end-to-end performance. Afore therefore treats reconfiguration not only as a placement problem, but also as a scheduling problem: it overlaps expert migration with the computation of preceding in-flight microbatches in the AFD pipeline, reducing the reconfiguration overhead exposed to serving. Right: Corresponding output throughput under the same configurations. 3 Case Study and Motivation We first present a controlled case study to understand how expert reconfiguration affects AFD-based MoE serving, where we focus on three key questions: • Question 1: whether static expert placement is sufficient under dynamic expert demand. • Question 2: whether microbatch-level demand prefetching can improve reconfiguration decisions. • Question 3: whether the pipeline execution of AFD can hide expert migration overhead. Experiment setup. We serve a 110B-parameter MoE model ( GLM-4.5-Air ) on a cluster of 16 NVIDIA A100 GPUs under a PD+AFD deployment. The cluster is partitioned into 4 prefill workers, 4 attention/routing workers, and 8 FFN/expert workers; the FFN side uses expert parallelism degree 8. We replay a dynamic serving workload in which the expert-token distribution varies across microbatches. All configurations use the same model, workload, GPU allocation, batching policy, and FFN expert-parallel layout. We compare four configurations: ( i ) static expert placement, ( ii ) expert reconfiguration without prefetch or overlap, ( iii ) expert reconfiguration with prefetch but without overlap, and ( iv ) expert reconfiguration with prefetch and overlap. We report end-to-end throughput and inter-token latency in Figure 3 . Baseline approach: static expert placement. We first evaluate static expert placement, where experts are evenly partitioned across the 8 FFN workers at initialization, and the placement remains fixed throughout serving. This configuration introduces no migration overhead, but it cannot adapt to changes in expert demand dynamics. As shown in Figure 3 , the baseline reaches 11,357.31 tokens/s throughput and 341.713 ms P95 inter-token latency. Its mean token-assignment EP load imbalance ratio is 1.70 × \times , causing the FFN stage to wait for overloaded workers. Approach 1: expert reconfiguration without prefetch or overlap. We next evaluate dynamic expert reconfiguration without using demand prefetching or migration overlap. For a target microbatch m t m_{t} in FFN execution order, let d t d_{t} denote its per-expert demand and d h ⁡ ( t ) d_{h(t)} the demand observed at the same layer and microbatch position in the preceding serving step. This approach uses d h ⁡ ( t ) d_{h(t)} rather than d t d_{t} to identify historical hot experts and adjust their placement. When a reconfiguration decision is made, the system migrates the selected experts and applies the new placement before executing m t m_{t} . Compared with Static, this approach lowers the mean token-assignment EP load imbalance ratio from 1.70 × \times to 1.42 × \times (a 16.7% reduction), improves throughput by 4.5%, and reduces P95 inter-token latency by 3.9%. Insight 1: dynamic reconfiguration is necessary. The improvement over Static shows that expert placement should not remain fixed under dynamic MoE workloads. Even a simple history-based policy can reduce FFN-stage stragglers by moving hot experts away from overloaded workers. This confirms that expert reconfiguration is necessary for maintaining FFN-stage balance in AFD-based MoE serving. Approach 2: expert reconfiguration with prefetch but without overlap. We then isolate the benefit of microbatch-level demand prefetching. Instead of relying on historical demand d h ⁡ ( t ) d_{h(t)} , this approach uses the target microbatch’s actual demand d t d_{t} to guide expert placement. Compared with Approach 1, it lowers the mean token-assignment EP load imbalance ratio from 1.42 × \times to 1.10 × \times (a 22.2% reduction), as shown in the left panel of Figure 4 . It also improves throughput by 7.1% and reduces P95 inter-token latency by 3.0%. Insight 2: prefetching improves reconfiguration quality. History-based reconfiguration can reduce persistent imbalance, but it may still adapt to stale load patterns when expert demand changes quickly. Microbatch-level prefetching exposes the actual expert demand of upcoming execution, allowing the approach to choose placements that better match the workload about to enter the FFN stage. This validates O1 in § 1 . Approach 3: expert reconfiguration with prefetch and overlap. Finally, we evaluate expert reconfiguration with both demand prefetching and migration overlap. This approach uses the same prefetched expert-token distribution as Approach 2, but starts expert migration as soon as the target microbatch’s demand becomes available. The migration overlaps with the FFN-stage computation of preceding in-flight microbatches; the target uses the new placement after the required copies complete. Compared with Approach 2, this approach reduces mean exposed migration wait by 100%, improves throughput by 16.4%, and reduces P95 inter-token latency by 11.8%.
